sentences.text: Everything a net brings up that is not a fish gets thrown back, and Iro had been throwing it back since she was seven.
That was the job.
It was her job on her uncle's boat and it had been her mother's job on the same boat and it was, as far as Iro could tell, the entry-level position in the whole of the eastern Aegean.
You stand at the sorting table with the catch coming out of the net and you pull out what does not belong, and the fish go one way and the rest goes over the side.
The rest is mostly weed and stones and plastic.
Mostly plastic, if she is honest, and the proportion had changed in her lifetime in a way that nobody on that boat ever said out loud.
Her uncle had a word for the whole category and the word was not complimentary and it covered a fifteenth-century amphora sherd and a supermarket bag equally.
But not entirely.

Over six years Iro had put back a bicycle wheel, a printer, a great many single shoes, a mannequin's arm that had caused a considerable amount of shouting, and, on one morning in the March she was ten, a brass compass with a cracked glass that had made her uncle stop what he was doing and hold it for a while and then say, "Over." She had said it seemed a shame.
"It's a compass with no glass off a boat that sank before I was born," he said.
"What do you want me to do with it?
Put it in the house?" There was a version of the argument Iro could have made and did not, at ten, because she did not have the words for it yet.
It was that the compass was not rubbish and was not treasure and that the boat had no category for a third thing.
She had thought about that for years afterwards, because he was right and because she had also been right, and she had never worked out how both could be true at once.

The compass went over the side at about half past five in the morning three miles off Panormos, and Iro watched it go down through water so clear that she could follow it for what felt like an extremely long way.
And something came up and took it.
Not a fish.
Fish do not do that.

What came up out of the dark under the boat was pale and enormous and moved in a way that made her stomach turn over, and it came up perhaps four metres, and one arm went out and closed on the compass in mid-water, and the whole of it folded and was gone.
Iro did not say anything to her uncle.
She has never been able to explain why, and the closest she can get is that she was ten, and she had watched something happen that was clearly none of her business.
She thought about it for the rest of that day and most of that year.

The obvious explanation was the right one and she knew it even then: an octopus took a shiny object in mid-water, which is a thing they do, and which is on film, and which nobody who works on that sea would find worth mentioning at breakfast.
What stopped her was the timing.
It had come up before the compass reached it.

She had watched the brass going down and she had watched the pale thing coming up to meet it, and the two had arrived at the same point at the same moment, which meant it had started before it could have seen the compass at all.
It had started when the compass hit the water.
